Shoebridge indicates Greens wants digital duty of care passed without ministerial discretion
Greens leader David Shoebridge has indicated his party wants to see the passage of the government's digital duty of care but without the inclusion of ministerial discretion.
Labor has released an exposure draft of its digital duty of care, which would allow social media users to opt out of a social media algorithm.
It would also require big tech companies to mitigate and protect under-18s from harmful content, such as content that promotes hostile ideas about women.
But the current draft gives the communications minister the discretion to add to that list of harms, which has attracted criticism from the Coalition and Greens.

"The exposure draft had a number of concerns in it for us, particularly the extensive ministerial discretion proposed. But we've been on the record that we want to see this reform go through," Shoebridge says.

"I think there's a strong call to say that the likes of Meta and Google and others should be held to account when they cause harm. But we will be looking at the draft legislation, and I expect that's going to go through a process in parliament before it's finally legislated."
Key Event
Chalmers cleans up ATO credit card ban with funding to delay start date until next year
Freshly back from a trip to Japan, the treasurer is coming in hot, armed with a broom, to try and clean up the tax office's controversial credit card ban.
The ATO announced last week it would stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from December, in response to the Reserve Bank's ban on credit card surcharges.
The tax office justified the move saying it would cost $200 million a year to absorb the fees, and noted only five per cent of small businesses used credit cards to pay their tax bills anyway.
But small businesses weren't buying the argument, and even ministers were at odds over whether the ATO should reverse the decision.
Jim Chalmers is today expected to announce more funding for the ATO to delay the credit card ban for up to a year.
Taylor demands ATO reverse ban on credit card payments
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor is demanding the tax office reverse its ban on credit card payments.
The ATO is due to implement the change at the end of November following the Reserve Bank's decision to prohibit card surcharges.
Taylor is urging the government to direct the ATO make a change today. If not, he says the opposition will introduce legislation when parliament sits next week.

"It would say to the tax office that you've got to accept credit card payments. It would overturn the decision that's been made. It's pretty simple. It's not going to be a complicated piece of legislation," he says.
Any legislation introduced by the opposition would be unlikely to pass the parliament without government support, because they do not have the numbers in the House of Reps.
Taylor accuses Treasurer Jim Chalmers of being in hiding.
We're expecting Chalmers to hold a press conference of his own sometime within the next hour.
Greens reserve position on 30pc tax on discretionary trusts
The Greens haven't said whether they would support tax changes on discretionary trusts announced in this year's federal budget.
The Australian Financial Review reports Labor will introduce a bill to parliament next week to impose a 30 per cent tax on discretionary tax.
Greens leader David Shoebridge says the Greens are yet to see the final draft the of the legislation.
Speaking in Melbourne, Shoebridge says his party wants to make sure the bill makes people's lives "materially better" and doesn't give "huge loopholes" to business.

"There's a simple test if it's true to what they said, if it's making people's lives better, then it gets our support," Shoebridge says."But if they're back-pedalling in the face of pressure from One Nation again, well, they're going to probably have a difficult week."

Analysis: Unless you're Pauline Hanson, the migration debate can be a dangerous sinkhole
Way back when the opposition started talking about cutting immigration, it would have thought on the basis of polling it was tapping into a vein of political gold.
But since then, Pauline Hanson has taken ownership of the goldmine and pretty much locked it away for One Nation.
Simon Welsh, from the Redbridge Group political consultancy, says: "The Liberals talking about migration doesn't create more Liberal voters, it creates more One Nation voters.

"Immigration offers people a simple explanation for the pressures they are feeling. When the major parties talk about it, it validates that. [Voters] then ask, 'who is the strongest voice on immigration?' It's a massive strategic error [by the major parties]," Welsh says.
Also, and crucially, the opposition may not have initially appreciated how a migration policy can open a political sinkhole that it's easy to be pushed into and hard to scramble out of.
We're seeing that this week, now Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has finally released the Coalition's plan.

AFP commissioner raises alarm about impact of tech-enabled crime on children's safety
The federal police commissioner says Australia needs to consider the rapidly shifting artificial intelligence (AI) environment and the impact on children's safety.
Some children as young as 12 are being manipulated through AI-altered nude images and sadistic online exploitation.
An Adelaide University study has found one in three Australian children who are sexually victimised online tell no-one or turn to an AI chatbot for help.
AFP Commissioner Krissy Barrett has stopped short of endorsing the federal government's digital duty of care bill.
But she told ABC Radio National Breakfast that tech-enabled cybercrime is becoming a growing part of her agency's workload.
"We know AI can be very useful for many things, but … AI is not somewhere where young kids should be going to get advice," Barrett says.

"In the last 12 months ... we have seen just the rapid increase in the use of AI and tech-enabled crime that is becoming part of our caseload."So that means that we all have a responsibility to continue to consider how do we best protect our kids in the online space."

Greens senator says Labor should force banks to wear cost of credit card surcharges
Greens senator Steph Hodgins-May says the government needs to regulate to ensure banks carry the costs of credit card surcharges.
The Reserve Bank has banned credit card surcharges, which businesses say they have either been forced to absorb or pass on to customers.
Businesses have raised concerns about the tax office's decision to end credit card payments following the surcharge ban.
Speaking to ABC Radio National Breakfast, Hodgins-May says the government should force banks to wear the costs of card transactions.

"Labor needs to put down rules that will protect business, small business who are already doing it incredibly tough at this point, and also the greed of big banks. They need to regulate the banks," Hodgins-May says.

"This falls back on Labor. It was as predictable, I'd say, as the sun rising. And they have a responsibility in the depths of a cost-of-living crisis to regulate the banks and ensure that this does not get pushed on to consumers and to small business."
Small business group calls for ATO to delay payment plans
The peak organisation representing small business has called on the tax office to delay payments for businesses on a payment plan so they can adjust to a decision to end credit card payments.
The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) has moved to end credit card payments for tax bills after the Reserve Bank's decision to end surcharges.
Business groups have raised concerns at the move, and have argued some businesses use credit cards to help manage cash flow.
Council of Small Business Organisations Australia (COSBOA) chair Matthew Addison has told ABC Radio National Breakfast there's inconsistency in the government's approach.

"I'm not saying forgive their tax, but just delay their payment plan for a month. Why were they using credit cards? To help manage their cash flow," Addison says."They're going to cease that cash flow control through credit cards. They need to give them a month's delay in their payment plans."
"I'm not saying forgive their tax, but just delay their payment plan for a month. Why were they using credit cards? To help manage their cash flow," Addison says.
"They're going to cease that cash flow control through credit cards. They need to give them a month's delay in their payment plans."
Matt Canavan says migration system is not 'making anymore new Australians'
Matt Canavan says the Coalition's migration plan will return Australia's migration system to one that offers people a permanent home.
The Coalition announced plans to drastically cut back migration targeting graduate, refugee and bridging visas.
Under a Coalition government, net overseas migration will be reduced to 100,000 in the first two years of government, before rising to 130,000 in the third and 160,000 in the fourth year.
But sectors, including in aged care, have raised concerns the plan could lead to a shortage of critical workers.
The Nationals leader has told ABC Radio National Breakfast that he feels the current migration system doesn't allow people to set down roots in Australia.

"I think we have a country and we've had a successful migration program that's been based on offering people here a permanent home, a new start, a new life, they can create a new family and they become new Australians," Canavan says."And right now, the problem with the migration program is we're not actually making anymore new Australians as we did before."

"And right now, the problem with the migration program is we're not actually making anymore new Australians as we did before."
AFP chief says policing alone can't fix rise in online child abuse
More than one in three Australian children who are sexually victimised online either tell no-one or turn to an AI chatbot for help, according to data from Adelaide University.
The data has prompted Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett to warn law enforcement cannot be the only safety net for vulnerable young people.

In an interview marking her first year in the top job, Commissioner Barrett stopped short of directly endorsing an extension of the federal government's under-16 social media ban to AI chatbots, but stressed that "anything that helps to keep our kids safer is obviously something we support".
The study, an initiative between Adelaide University and the AFP-led Australian Centre to Counter Child Exploitation, has delivered sobering data on how generative tools are altering youth safety.

Key Event
Wong says Australia has made representations to Vietnam over arrest of Australian activist
Foreign Minister Penny Wong says Australia has made representations to Vietnam over the case of an Australian human rights activist charged in the South-East Asian country.

Vietnamese authorities have charged Australian human rights activist Hiep Tran and his Norwegian-Vietnamese colleague Duc Thuan Nguyen over an alleged plot to carry out terrorist activities in the country.
US-based pro-democracy group Viet Tan disputes the accusations and believes the men were abducted in an act of "transnational repression".
Speaking to ABC News Breakfast, Wong has confirmed she's aware of the matter but says it's not a topic she'll engage on due to privacy reasons.

"I have dealt with quite a lot of people over the period of time I have been foreign minister to date. I'm careful what I say publicly. We have made representations in the way that we think is most effective for the person concerned," Wong says.
"We know that different political regimes in the region have very different approaches to individual freedom and political freedom to that that Australia takes."
Watt says ministers will be reinforcing views with ATO on payment changes
Murray Watt says the "various ministers" will be making their expectations clear to the tax office about its decision to ban credit card payments.
Business groups have voiced outrage at the Australian Tax Office's (ATO) decision to end credit card payments for the payment of tax bills.
Yesterday, the housing minister and assistant science minister gave differing views on Labor's position about the payment ban.
Speaking to Channel Seven, the environment minister says government ministers will be reinforcing their views about the ATO's decision.

"We need to keep it in perspective, that when it comes to payments to the ATO, it's only a very small number of taxpayers who pay their tax payments by credit card. It's about 5 per cent for small businesses and about 2 per cent for individuals," Watt says.

"We were very clear with the ATO when they first proposed this, that they needed to have a transition plan, that they needed to work properly with the business community. And I'm sure that those expectations will be reinforced."
Joining the environment minister on the political panel today is deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume, who says the government can change the decision "with the stroke of a pen".
"You can't blame the ATO. They're your agency. You're the government. You can do this," Hume says.
Key Event
Wong says govt can't intervene and force ATO to reverse end to credit card payments
Penny Wong says the government doesn't have the power to direct the tax office to reverse its decision to stop accepting credit card payments.
The Coalition has called on Labor to direct the department to reverse the change so businesses can use credit cards to make tax payments.
The Australian Taxation Office made the decision to stop accepting credit card payments after the Reserve Bank ended surcharges.
But speaking to Channel Nine, Wong says the government can't intervene because the ATO is independent.
"In terms of the ATO, I'd make two points. They are independent. Governments can't direct tax office, the tax office to implement tax in a certain way," Wong says.

"What we can do is say to them, you should be consulting with small business, and we would really encourage the ATO to engage with small business about this."I know that only a small proportion of small businesses were using credit cards for this, but obviously it is a change."
"What we can do is say to them, you should be consulting with small business, and we would really encourage the ATO to engage with small business about this.
"I know that only a small proportion of small businesses were using credit cards for this, but obviously it is a change."
Key Event
Conroy says Labor ministers have been 'appropriately urging' ATO to consult business
Pat Conroy has moved to smooth over the response from Labor ministers about the Australian Tax Office's (ATO) decision to stop accepting credit card payments.
The ATO has maintained its position to stop accepting credit card payments for tax bills from December 1, after the Reserve Bank banned credit card surcharges from the start of this month.
Yesterday, Clare O'Neil told Channel Nine that Labor had "real concerns" about the ATO's decision to end credit card payments.
"Small businesses across the country are really struggling to manage their cash flow," she said yesterday.
But soon after, Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton told ABC Radio Labor supported the ATO's decision to ban credit card tax payments.
The defence industry minister has defended the end of credit card surcharges on Channel Nine this morning, but says it's up to the ATO to work with businesses to find a solution.

"What Labor ministers have been doing is appropriately urging the ATO to consult with small businesses. This is about transparency for consumers. That's what the broader decision is about," Conroy says.

"But the broader point is there, consumers want transparency. When I go to a shop, the price should be the same whether I pay with cash or card, so that people know that going in. And that's what the decision from the Reserve Bank is all about."
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says there's "open warfare" in the government over the ATO's decision.
"I guess the question is who is actually in charge at the moment. The prime minister in the Pacific, we've got the treasurer off in Japan," he says.
